Row 6 · Generation 3 · Nov 11

Onboarding shaped by a real evaluation: Resend

We ran the full product-eval methodology on Resend (5 features × CLI / self-hosted MCP / hosted MCP, Claude Code + Codex, 30 runs) and restructured it into parent prompts with scenarios. These three options turn that path into onboarding. Example data on every screen is Resend's real setup and results.

Methodology steps → where they live
  • Discover surfaces (CLI, MCP, API, SDK, docs) → A1 · B left · C1
  • User picks + who uses it (agents, capability) → A1
  • Setup: install + auth in one step → A3 access card
  • Local vs cloud → MCP self-hosted vs hosted lanes
  • Find ~5 core features → A2 · B rows
  • Starting state (blank vs existing app) → A2
  • Prompt in user words, checks carry the knowledge → A2 preview · C2
  • Run + read → A3 · A4
Lessons from Resend built in (each was a bug in our first 30 runs)
  • Scenario per surface, named in the text: an unnamed CLI lane only measured discovery (1/10).
  • Per-run ids in fixtures; runs staggered, never 30 at once on one account.
  • Persona instructions off unless a browser is needed (the login hint leaked into Codex's task).
  • End goal must match the prompt text (two features scored 0/6 on unstated steps).
  • n ≥ 3 per cell before quoting rates.
The three options
A · Guided plan (4 screens)
Methodology as a wizard: surfaces → jobs → plan → first result. Most explicit, best for a devrel lead who wants to see the matrix before spending runs.
B · One matrix (1 screen)
Everything on one page: features × surfaces grid, setup on the left, run budget on the right. Fastest for someone who already knows what they ship.
C · Agent-led (2 screens)
The user's coding agent builds the plan over the Firegoat MCP; the dashboard shows the live plan and a plan check that flags the Resend-style mistakes before anything runs. Extends Gen 2's MCP-first entry.

Suggested: C as the default entry (matches Gen 2 screen 1), with A's plan screen (A3) as the approval view, and B as "edit plan" for power users.

frames.name: Onboarding flows — overview
frames.html:
Onboarding flows — overview

Three onboarding flows for 2027 evals. Each one is built around a different question the user wants answered, and each uses only backend calls that exist today. Anything that would need new backend is tagged needs backend on its screen. Below this frame: Flow A (row 1), Flow B (row 2), Flow C (row 3). Every screen has a grey strip that names the existing call behind it.
The three flows
Flow A · 7 screens · row 1
“Can a coding agent actually use my CLI or MCP, start to finish?”
Who
A devrel or DX lead at a company that ships a CLI, MCP server or SDK (Neon, Clerk, Expo). Knows what they ship, not what an “eval prompt” is.
Problem
“I don't know where agents give up on our tool: install, login, or the task itself.”
Measures
Install → login → task, step by step. Custom checks in the user's words (“Used the Neon CLI”, “Logged in”, “App reads from the DB”) on top of the 8 defaults.
Entry
Pick CLI / MCP / API / Docs / Something else, then paste the install line. This is the flow's one monospace input.
Screens
  1. What do you want agents to use?
  2. Install command (or MCP config / URL)
  3. Sandbox findings: commands, login method, exit codes
  4. Pick one of 2 suggested tasks
  5. How the agent logs in (token / browser agent / nothing)
  6. What counts as done (custom checks)
  7. Run it and follow along
Hands off
“Try it on competitors” → Flow B · “Rerun without the token” → discovery run
Flow B · 7 screens · row 2
“How do we compare to competitors on the same task?”
Who
A founder or PM who wants a positioning claim they can defend (“agents ship on Neon more reliably than on Supabase”).
Problem
“A comparison only counts if everyone got the same task, the same checks and the same way in.”
Measures
One prompt with one competitor lane per provider: goal met n/N per lane, per-check squares, where each lane got stuck, and the one shared login mode shown in the header.
Entry
Pick an existing prompt that names your product. A new one-line task goes through Flow A's steps 2–4.
Screens
  1. Which task to compare on (unsuitable prompts greyed out, with the reason)
  2. Who are you up against (each lane's rewritten prompt)
  3. Is it a fair fight? Login mode per lane, with “Match all”
  4. What counts as done for everyone (vendor-only checks flagged)
  5. Attempts per provider vs. trial quota
  6. Live lane grid
  7. Results land on the Benchmarking tab
Hands off
Add attempts · Rerun every lane with keys · Add a competitor
Flow C · 6 screens · row 3
“I just have a URL. Tell me how agents experience my product.”
Who
A first-touch signup with only a website. Doesn't know yet whether they're “a CLI”, “an API” or “just docs”.
Problem
“Run one honest attempt, then show me where it got stuck and what would get it further.”
Measures
One attempt on the obvious first task (the getting-started guide), scored on the 8 default checks plus “where it got stuck”. No headline score.
Entry
Website only, prefilled from the sign-in domain. No install or config input, so no monospace field.
Screens
  1. What's your website?
  2. Here's what we think you ship (offers Flow A if a CLI or MCP is found)
  3. What should a new developer try first?
  4. Should the agent get a head start? (discover / key / browser agent)
  5. Follow your first eval
  6. Your first result: where it got stuck and 3 next steps
Hands off
Add key and rerun · Test your CLI → Flow A · Compare → Flow B
Brief coverage. Choose what to evaluate: A·1 (C·2 sends you there when a CLI or MCP is found). Install / config input: A·2. Sandbox scan proposing 1–2 prompts: A·3–4 (C·3 suggests one). AI setup help: the A·3 chat agent drives the sandbox. Keys, login and browser agent on/off: A·5, B·3 and C·4, which share one “who does what” card pattern. Custom checks: A·6 and B·4. Follow the eval live: A·7, B·6, C·5. Comparing providers on the same prompt: all of Flow B.

Real issue found while mocking (Flow B), confirmed in code. resolveEvalContext lets any child with env: null inherit the parent's env, competitor lanes included. Login hints are fenced by target provider; env is not. So a lane created by add_competitor runs with the parent's NEON_API_KEY, and it fires before the user can change it. That is unfair by default and sends your key to a competitor's task. Flow B defaults lanes to env:{}. Worth a bead whatever onboarding we pick.
Recommendation

Build Flow C first, then A, then B.

Why C first:

  • It's the front door with the worst experience. 189 of 764 active customer prompts are open-ended getting-started prompts, spread over 43 orgs, the most orgs of any category. They succeed 25% of the time, and the browser agent runs in 66% of them. Users land here and don't understand the result. C·4 (“Should the agent get a head start?”) explains exactly that.
  • It runs almost entirely on today's backend: provider.scan → create_prompt → update_prompt_config → request_run → RunStatusView. Its needs-backend items (typed scan rows, live steps) can be hidden without losing the flow.
  • It builds the shared parts: the “who logs in” card (reused in A·5 and B·3) and the run ladder (A·7, B·6). Its result screen already links into A and B, so those can ship later as branches.

Then A. CLI has the highest hard-fail rate (14–20%) and MCP gains 35 points with keys. A·3's sandbox check works today via the chat agent (create_sandbox / run_command). Check generation and MCP connection are the backend asks.

Then B, after the lane-env fix above. Without that fix, every comparison it produces is skewed, and today's backend can't stop it.

Not covered by any flow: dashboard / account-flow prompts (14). They need the browser agent and are not a first-run case.
